You shouldn't have just stopped paying. You should have arranged with the Court to make your payments to the Court, which the Court will then hold in its registry (or equivalent term in your state) until your case is heard. The Court would then determine if you have the right to your money back or if it should be paid to the landlord.

If you are actually going to appeal this, as part of a good faith effort to show that you want to participate in this process, arrange to place the rent money in the registry when you file your appeal. I am a lawyer, although not licensed in PA, which is important because the laws governing housing are jurisdiction dependent. You have legitimate complaints if the condition of the house is as you say, and provided you can prove that you brought these complaints to the notice of the landlord. However, in most jurisdictions, stopping the paying of rent is not allowed as a recourse for an inattentive landlord. You entered a legal contract to rent the house. Yes, local laws require the house to be habitable, but most of the time that does not give you the right to break your contract without recourse by the landlord.

First you should have documented your complaints to the landlord, if you did not do so. Second, you should take these complaints to your local housing authority if the landlord is unresponsive. Thirdly, you should seek the advice of an attorney for any compensation that might be due to neglected housing violations. However, at no point should you have stopped paying the full amount of rent until you were instructed to do so by someone with authority to legally rule on the matter.
